newsitem.title: UK: Scottish finance houses wary of devolution plans.
newsitem.headline: Scottish finance houses wary of devolution plans.

text.p: Scotland's financial community, now reporting record levels of UK and international funds under management, is warning about the impact of plans to let Scotland go its own way which are being debated ahead of the election.
Data for 1995, the latest available, show the sector recorded an inflow of funds of 170 billion stg, a 25 percent rise on the year before.
Fund managers expect 1996 and 1997 to produce similar growth but also political, economic and constitutional change which could threaten its traditional niche in financial markets.

Business lobby group Scottish Financial Enterprise (SFE) has been holdings a series of meetings recently between financiers and senior Labour politicians. At one in Edinburgh, where the opposition Labour Party plans a Scottish Parliament or Assembly, Shadow Treasury chief secretary Alistair Darling was urged to approach the devolution issue with caution.
He replied that corporate Scotland would "be treated the same as everybody else in Britain" under Labour. "It would be nonsense to make somebody cope with two different financial systems," he added.
Sir John Shaw, SFE chairman, said uncertainty prevailed. "Although it has been modified by these assurances, we do still need clarity on what devolution actually means to the sector."
Shaw, who is also deputy governor of Bank of Scotland, wanted more information of what the Secretary of State for Scotland would do and the structure of a Scottish Assembly.
The financial management industry is still divided as to the implications of greater political autonomy for Scotland.

Allan McKenzie, director of Scottish Widows Investment Management (SWIM), which has some 24 billion stg under management, said, "We cannot afford to contemplate our navels. We have to think UK and global...I do not subscribe to the tartan card (devolution). It represents a false sense of security."

Although SWIM is building its new headquarters in Edinburgh 90 percent of its business comes from England. "If anything was ever done to compromise our competitiveness, we would have to look at our position," McKenzie added.
Darling has visited SWIM as part of the party's 18-month drive to woo financiers, usually deeply sceptical of Labour. McKenzie described him as "a very sensible chap."
Iain Watt, chairman of Edinburgh Fund Managers, noted there had been a lack of debate about the benefits or risks associated with devolution, and called for a longer term outlook.
"Scotland has done very well over the last 10-15 years but what about the next decade?" he asked. "The trouble with politicians is they don't look far enough forward.
"We are Scots but this does not mean we do not think London, or Switzerland or Boston. What is crucial is that we must maintain at all times our edge as fund managers."
Watt said: "With a distinct legal system and superb place to live, the country could finish up operating as a tax haven for offshore investments."

Willie Watt, a Scottish director of venture capital company 3i which is involved in 75 percent of all deals in Scotland said: "Personally, I think Labour would be insane to suggest any increase in taxes, especially income tax."
